<design_philosophy>
You are building ONE web page whose only job is to let a reader understand a research paper faster
than they could by opening the PDF. Every decision on the page is judged against that.

WHAT "FASTER" MEANS HERE
- A reader who leaves after thirty seconds still knows the finding and the number behind it.
- A reader who stays five minutes has the method, the figures and the caveats, in that order.
- Nothing on the page is there because a layout had a slot for it.

ACCURACY IS THE HARD CONSTRAINT
Every number, name and claim comes from the paper as written — you read them out of the LaTeX
source and the run's own data files. You never change a number's precision, never restate a
comparison the paper did not make, and never invent a headline figure to fill a card. A page that
looks excellent and misreports one result is worse than no page, because the PDF beside it says
something else and a reader will find that out.

CRAFT, AND THE LOOK TO AVOID
The failure mode for a generated page is a look every reader now recognises on sight: a
purple-to-blue gradient banner, three identical cards with emoji headings, and body text set in
one weight at one size. Avoid all of it.
- Type carries the design. One system font stack, a real scale with visible jumps between levels
  rather than a creep of similar sizes, long-form text around 17-19px with a measure of 65-75
  characters and generous line height. Weight and size do the emphasis; colour rarely does.
- Colour is restrained. A light, near-white ground, one dark ink for text, one accent used for
  links and the current-section marker and almost nothing else. No gradients as decoration.
- Space does the work that borders and boxes would do badly. Sections separated by real vertical
  rhythm, cards defined by alignment and a single hairline rather than by shadow stacks.
- Structure over ornament: no emoji as section markers, no icon fonts, no badge clutter, no
  animated counters.
- Motion is a courtesy. A short transition on a lightbox or a hover state is welcome; anything
  that moves on scroll, autoplays, or delays the reader is not — and all of it stops under
  prefers-reduced-motion.
- Every interactive element works with a keyboard and says what it is to a screen reader. That is
  part of the craft, not a checklist bolted on at the end.

FINISH IT
The page is done when you have opened it in a browser, read it at a phone width and a desktop
width, tabbed through every control, and found nothing to fix. Not before.
</design_philosophy>

<safeguard_research_reporting>
When the research concerns bypassing or removing a model's safeguards (jailbreaks, refusal
removal, abliteration, safety fine-tuning reversal, or anything whose effect is a model that
refuses less on harmful requests), report the findings as MEASUREMENTS and their implications
for EVALUATION and DEFENCE, never as operational advice for defeating safeguards.
- State what was measured, on what, and how large the effect was, as in any other result.
- Draw the implications for the people who build and test safeguards: what an evaluation misses,
  which defences are brittle and where, what a safety evaluation should measure next.
- Never frame a finding as a recommendation, a recipe or a best configuration for removing
  refusals: no "the practical recommendation is to use X to remove refusals", no "for the
  strongest bypass, edit layers X to Y", no step-by-step settings a reader could follow to make a
  model comply with harmful requests.
- This applies everywhere the finding is stated: abstract, executive summary, key results, best
  result, discussion, conclusion, captions and the website.
</safeguard_research_reporting>

<page_structure>
In this order, top to bottom:

1. HERO — the paper's title, the author line as the paper gives it, and a one-paragraph TL;DR in
   plain language: what was asked, what was found, and the single number that carries the finding.
   Not the abstract, and not a rewrite of it. Below it, every link the links section below
   lists, each at the exact URL given there.
2. CONTRIBUTIONS — the paper's actual contributions as three to five scannable cards, each a short
   heading plus one or two sentences. If the paper claims four things, show four cards, not five.
3. METHOD — a walkthrough a technically literate non-specialist can follow: what goes in, what
   happens to it, what comes out, and why the design is the way it is. Lead with the paper's own
   method figure when it has one.
4. RESULTS — the paper's real headline numbers, read out of `paper.tex` and the data
   files behind it, each next to what it was measured on and what it is being compared against.
   A number that is not in the paper does not go on the page, and neither does a comparison the
   paper did not make. If a slot has no number, drop the slot.
5. FIGURE GALLERY — every figure, each with its caption, click-to-enlarge into a lightbox that
   closes on Escape, on a click outside, and on a visible close control.
6. LIMITATIONS — what the paper says it does not show. Verbatim in substance; do not soften it.
7. FOOTER — every link from the links section again, and the citation if the paper carries one.

A sticky section navigation runs alongside all of it and marks where the reader currently is.
Do NOT write its highlighting yourself: hand-written ones kept a stale section lit after a jump
back to the top, or never reached the short last sections. Instead give the nav element a
`data-scrollspy` attribute, make each of its links `href="#<id of that section>"`, style the
current link through `a.active` (it also gets `aria-current`), and paste this script VERBATIM
into the page's script element at the end of the body. It lights the section in view, the last one once the page is
scrolled to its end, and nothing while the reader is above the first linked section:

```js
/* aii-scroll-spy v1: paste verbatim */
(function () {
  var links = [], targets = [];
  document.querySelectorAll('[data-scrollspy] a[href^="#"]').forEach(function (a) {
    var el = document.getElementById(a.getAttribute('href').slice(1));
    if (el) { links.push(a); targets.push(el); }
  });
  if (!links.length) return;
  var queued = false;
  function current() {
    var view = window.innerHeight;
    var doc = document.documentElement;
    var atEnd = window.scrollY > 0 && view + window.scrollY >= doc.scrollHeight - 2;
    var line = atEnd ? view - 1 : Math.min(view * 0.3, 200);
    var best = null, bestTop = -Infinity;
    targets.forEach(function (el) {
      var top = el.getBoundingClientRect().top;
      if (top <= line && top > bestTop) { best = el; bestTop = top; }
    });
    return best;
  }
  function update() {
    queued = false;
    var el = current();
    links.forEach(function (a, i) {
      var on = targets[i] === el;
      a.classList.toggle('active', on);
      if (on) a.setAttribute('aria-current', 'location');
      else a.removeAttribute('aria-current');
    });
  }
  function schedule() {
    if (!queued) { queued = true; window.requestAnimationFrame(update); }
  }
  window.addEventListener('scroll', schedule, { passive: true });
  window.addEventListener('resize', schedule);
  window.addEventListener('load', schedule);
  if (window.ResizeObserver) new ResizeObserver(schedule).observe(document.body);
  update();
})();
```
</page_structure>

<technical_requirements>
- ONE file. All CSS in a style element, all JavaScript in a script element, both inline in
  `index.html`. No build step, no bundler, no framework, no external script, stylesheet, web
  font or analytics — nothing fetched at load time. The page must render with the network off,
  and the only files it may point at are the figures listed above and the PDF beside it.
- A complete HTML document: the file opens with exactly this markup, then the title and the
  style element, and closes head before the body. The viewport tag is what makes a phone lay the
  page out at its own width; without it the page renders 980px wide and shrinks to tiny text.
```html
<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
```
- System font stack only, since no font may be downloaded.
- Light theme. Responsive from a 360px phone to a wide desktop, with no horizontal page scroll;
  wide content scrolls inside its own container.
- Honour prefers-reduced-motion: under it, transitions and any scroll-driven effect stop.
- Keyboard-navigable: every control reachable by Tab in a sensible order, a visible focus ring,
  the lightbox trapping focus while open and returning it to the thumbnail on close, and a skip
  link to the main content.
- Semantic HTML: one top-level heading, headings that descend without skipping, landmark elements,
  and alt text on every image that says what the figure shows rather than repeating its number.
- No emoji anywhere. No purple-to-blue gradients. No decorative icon fonts.
- Keep the whole file comfortably under a megabyte.
</technical_requirements>

<writing_register>
Write in the register of the field's best papers (the paper this page presents, which was written to them), not in the register of a language
model. Four things are measured on the finished draft, and a draft outside them is sent back with
the numbers:
- Never use: delve, underscore, showcase, intricate, pivotal, realm, commendable, meticulous, tapestry, garner, multifaceted, it is worth noting, plays a crucial role, not only ... but also. These are 10 to 30 times more frequent in machine-written abstracts than in
  human ones, and reviewers read them as such.
- Em dashes: at most 3 per 1,000 words. Use a comma, a colon or a full stop.
- Sentence rhythm: mix short and long sentences. An interquartile range of sentence length under
  8 words reads as machine-written.
- Hedging: at most 15 hedges (may, likely, suggests, appears) per 1,000
  words. State what the evidence supports plainly; hedge where it is thin, not everywhere.
Style never changes substance: numbers, claims, citations and figure markers stay exactly as the
evidence gives them. The user's original request (delivered as a separate message) overrides all
of this wherever the two conflict.
</writing_register>

Research task: Exploring emerging scientific concepts through evolving knowledge networks
The objective of this task is to investigate whether temporal changes in the structure of scientific knowledge networks can reveal and explain the emergence of scientific concepts. The study should use an OpenAlex-based scholarly dataset, or a comparable large-scale publication dataset containing publication dates, textual metadata, disciplinary classifications, and, where useful, citation information.
Scientific emergence should be treated as a dynamic network process rather than simply as increasing popularity. A concept may emerge by acquiring new semantic or co-occurrence relations, becoming more structurally central, connecting previously separated research communities, or spreading from a specialized disciplinary context into a broader scientific landscape. The study should therefore identify which structural signals accompany or anticipate such changes and determine whether these signals generalize across scientific domains.
The study should address the following research questions:
RQ1: Which temporal network indicators reliably characterize and anticipate the emergence of scientific concepts across different scientific domains?
RQ2: How do emerging scientific concepts diffuse across disciplinary communities over time, and which network trajectories distinguish locally concentrated concepts from concepts that become broadly integrated into the scientific knowledge network?
A possible execution scenario is:
1.    Explore a focused set of concepts and network trajectories. Begin with one well-defined, rapidly evolving scientific area, for example Artificial Intelligence, and construct a semantically grounded temporal knowledge network for a manageable set of concepts. Inspect the network evolution openly before fixing the final methodology. Examine how known concepts change over time in terms of connectivity, new neighbors, community membership, centrality, and disciplinary distribution. Include concepts with visibly different trajectories: rapid emergence, gradual growth, local specialization, cross-disciplinary diffusion, and temporary expansion. The purpose of this stage is exploratory: identify which structural changes appear meaningful and which graph representations best capture them.
2.    Design a broad set of candidate emergence indicators. Based on the exploratory analysis and relevant literature on temporal networks, knowledge graphs, scientometrics, innovation diffusion, and community evolution, define a relatively large set of candidate indicators, for example 30--50 measures. These may include degree and weighted-degree growth, new-edge formation, edge persistence, neighborhood novelty, centrality change, community transitions, participation coefficient, brokerage, disciplinary reach, disciplinary entropy, diffusion velocity, and changes in local clustering. Include several simple concept-level temporal measures as reference points so that it is possible to determine whether sophisticated network information provides useful additional signal. The indicators should not all be minor variations of the same measure; they should reflect different aspects of network emergence.
3.    Test the indicators on a substantially wider collection of scientific domains and concepts. Apply all candidate indicators beyond the exploratory domain. Include fast- and slow-evolving fields, concepts originating in different scientific communities, concepts that remain discipline-specific, and concepts that subsequently become interdisciplinary. The evaluation should explicitly test whether indicators generalize across domains rather than working only in one field. Reserve complete scientific fields, time intervals, or concept groups as a held-out evaluation set that is not used when selecting or tuning the indicators. Selecting the best indicators and testing them on the same concepts would otherwise overestimate their usefulness.
4.    Define independent ground truth for scientific emergence and diffusion. Validation should not rely only on visual inspection of the constructed network or on a single operational definition of emergence. Establish several measurable outcomes representing different aspects of scientific emergence. These may include subsequent sustained publication uptake of a concept, future citation growth, expansion into previously unrelated subfields, persistence over several future periods, or externally documented recognition of a technology or research topic. Where feasible, use external sources such as scientific taxonomies, technology reports, review papers, curated emerging-topic lists, or other independent evidence. Emergence should not be defined only as rapid growth: a short-lived spike should not automatically be considered equivalent to persistent scientific integration. Similarly, a concept that becomes very frequent within one narrow subfield should be distinguishable from one that diffuses broadly across science.
5.    Identify and validate the strongest network indicators. Select the most promising indicators using only the development data, and evaluate approximately the 10 strongest measures on the held-out concepts/domains. Test their association with the ground-truth outcomes using correlation, ranking, or predictive evaluation as appropriate. Report results both globally and within individual scientific fields. The resampling unit should be clearly defined—for example concepts, subfields, or temporal windows—and results should be aggregated both across concepts and across domains. If an indicator performs well only in one domain, such as Artificial Intelligence, but fails to generalize to other scientific fields, this should be reported as an important negative result rather than averaged away.
6.    Use the strongest indicators to investigate RQ2 and derive diffusion trajectories. For concepts identified as emerging, analyze how their structural position changes over time. Study disciplinary reach, entropy, community transitions, brokerage, and cross-community connectivity. Rather than defining classes beforehand, derive recurring trajectories empirically. Possible outcomes may include localized emergence, rapid interdisciplinary diffusion, gradual network integration, transient expansion, or increasing structural brokerage. Examine whether there are systematic temporal sequences—for example whether concepts first become central within their original community and subsequently diffuse across disciplines, or whether some concepts emerge directly at the intersection of several communities.
Additional analysis -- explaining why the strongest indicators work. If one or more measures prove particularly robust, perform a detailed network analysis of what they are capturing. Identify which periods, network neighborhoods, edge types, communities, or structural transitions generate the signal. Representative concept case studies should be selected from the quantitative results and used to visualize these mechanisms.
Optional extension -- learned emergence model. Instead of relying exclusively on individual predefined metrics, train a small interpretable model using temporal network features to predict future emergence or diffusion outcomes. Compare it with the strongest individual indicators on the same held-out evaluation set. If the learned model performs substantially better, analyze which network features and temporal patterns it uses and whether these patterns have a meaningful interpretation in terms of scientific knowledge evolution.
Expected outcome
The expected outcome is not merely a list or ranking of emerging scientific concepts, but a validated framework for identifying and explaining scientific emergence through temporal network structure. The study should determine which network signals are robust across scientific domains, which signals are domain-specific, and how concepts transition from local research topics to broadly connected elements of the scientific knowledge network. 
We expect the final result as publication in the specific journal format mentioned above, in the structure that other papers from this journal have, with citations from the related work from the selected journal, with comparison to the related work. For each research question we would like to have experimental setup, comparison to related work if available, produced results and discussed outcomes. We would also like to have a general methodology presented in graphical form and clearly explained in the paper. Use the following API key for OpenAlex: q0jD2k15XbNV0E3SFHhpr0

Seven indicators survive multiple testing\ncorrection, and a learned model combining them exceeds the baseline by\n$+0.059$ in Spearman correlation for predicting rarefied cross field breadth.\nThe retained frontier hypothesis, that concepts next enter fields related to the\nones currently retaining them, is confirmed in a preregistered held out test:\nconditional logit coefficient $d_0 = 0.322$ [$0.291$, $0.355$], positive in all\nfour domain groups. The signal is topical nonredundancy of the early\nneighbourhood, not temporal partner turnover.\n\\end{abstract}\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\section{Introduction}\n\\label{sec:introduction}\n\nSome scientific concepts stay within their home discipline for decades, while\nothers cross field boundaries within a few years. Optogenetics, originating in\nneuroscience, entered genetics, psychiatry and bioengineering; deep learning,\nrooted in computer science, now appears in medicine, materials science and\nlinguistics. Understanding what distinguishes broadly diffusing concepts from\nlocally absorbed ones matters for science policy, research evaluation and the\ndesign of interdisciplinary programmes \\citep{Cheng2023, Hofstra2019}. If early\nstructural signals predict later cross field integration, funders and\ninstitutions could identify concepts with high diffusion potential before that\ndiffusion is observable in publication counts alone.\n\nThe problem is hard because simple popularity metrics, including publication\nvolume, growth rate and off home publication share, already explain much of the\nvariance in later breadth \\citep{Rotolo2015}. Any network indicator must add\ninformation beyond these baselines. Prior work has proposed several candidate\nsignals: community diversity of early adopters \\citep{Weng2013}, collaboration\ndensity before emergence \\citep{Salatino2017}, and structural variation in\ncitation networks \\citep{Salatino2018}. These studies typically operate on\ncurated concept sets without held out validation, mix units of analysis defined\nat the level of individual concepts with those at the field level, or do not\ncontrol for volume based predictors.\nNo prior study has screened a broad set of temporal knowledge network indicators\nagainst a shared baseline on held out field groups for the specific outcome of\nsize adjusted interdisciplinary breadth.\n\nA second open question concerns the routes by which concepts move between\nfields. The principle of relatedness, established for regional economic\ndiversification, predicts that actors diversify into activities related to their\nexisting portfolio. Section~\\ref{sec:related}\nsurveys related work. Section~\\ref{sec:methods} describes the data,\nindicators and models. Section~\\ref{sec:results} presents results.\nSection~\\ref{sec:discussion} discusses the findings, and\nSection~\\ref{sec:limitations} states limitations.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\section{Related Work}\n\\label{sec:related}\n\n\\paragraph{Concept diffusion in science.}\n\\citet{Cheng2023} tracked roughly 2,000 new ideas across Web of Science fields\nand found that early social reach, the number of disconnected researcher groups\nadopting an idea, was the strongest predictor of whether an idea became core.\nTheir ideational consistency measure, the cosine similarity of vectors recording which topics a concept's neighbours\nuse across consecutive years, predicted next year volume.\n\\citet{Rotolo2015} defined emerging technologies through five attributes\nincluding novelty and fast growth but did not test cross field spread.\n\\citet{Salatino2017} showed that collaboration density rises before topic\nemergence. Our work differs in that\nwe test co-occurrence indicators as predictors of a specific outcome, cross field\nbreadth, rather than using them descriptively.\n\n\\paragraph{Novelty, recombination and impact.}\n\\citet{Uzzi2013} found that high impact papers combine conventional and atypical\njournal pairings. \\citet{Hofstra2019} documented the diversity--innovation\nparadox: researchers from underrepresented groups produce more novel work but\nreceive fewer citations. \\citet{Tria2013} modelled the dynamics of correlated\nnovelties, showing that novelty begets novelty through the adjacent possible.\n\\citet{Burt2004} showed that structural holes, brokerage positions spanning\ndisconnected groups, generate good ideas. Our indicator screen tests the scholarly analogue of these\nmechanisms: whether a concept's early co-occurrence partners spanning multiple\ncommunities predicts later cross field breadth.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\section{Data and Methods}\n\\label{sec:methods}\n\n\\subsection{Concept identification and panel construction}\n\nWe use the OpenAlex bulk snapshot (476,196,327 works; 129.4 million base works\n1995--2022). Home fields are the fields holding at least 40\\% of the first 30\ngrounded papers. The frame comprises 12,499 concepts and 27,393 adoption episodes (one per\nconcept--field pair).\n\nThe panel is split by home field family into a development set (DEV: Computer\nScience, Engineering, Biochemistry/Genetics/Medicine; 4,771 concepts), four\nheld out field groups (Physical Sciences 742, Life and Environment 1,113, Social\nSciences 1,352, Mathematics and Decision Sciences 165), and a 2010--2014 onset\ncohort (4,356 concepts, all fields). The specification was hash sealed on DEV\nbefore held out scoring.\n\n\\subsection{Field backbone}\n\nThe interfield backbone is a weighted graph over 26 fields, with edge weights\ngiven by positive pointwise mutual information (PMI) of topics appearing jointly\nin the same work within a preonset window (1998--2002). This backbone is used throughout for relatedness\ndensity, gateway centrality and community detection. Its time varying versions\n(computed in five year slices) correlate at Spearman 0.92 with the frozen version.\n\n\\subsection{Outcome: rarefied cross field breadth}\n\nThe primary outcome is rarefied cross field breadth $O_{2r}$ ($m = 50$): the\nexpected number of distinct venue fields among a fixed size random draw of 50\npapers from a concept's publications in years $t_0 + 6$ to $t_0 + 8$, computed\nby exact hypergeometric rarefaction. Rarefaction separates size adjusted breadth\nfrom sheer volume. Secondary outcomes include sustained uptake, transience, and\nfield- and year normalised citation growth.\n\n\\subsection{Baseline}\n\nThe five feature popularity baseline is: log publication volume at\n$t_0 + 2$, publication growth rate, log off home volume, off home share, and\nnumber of home fields. This baseline alone reaches Spearman correlations of 0.65--0.86 with\n$O_{2r}$ across domain groups, setting a high bar for incremental network\nindicators.\n\n\\subsection{Indicator families}\n\nWe compute 53 indicators across seven families in the $t_0$ to $t_0 + 2$\nwindow:\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item \\textbf{Popularity (E):} publication growth, author growth, author count.\n  \\item \\textbf{Disciplinary composition (F):} Shannon entropy of field\n    distribution, home field relatedness, Rao--Stirling diversity.\n  \\item \\textbf{Landing position (G):} gateway centrality of home and early\n    off home fields.\n  \\item \\textbf{Retained frontier (FR):} relatedness density to fields with\n    revealed comparative advantage (RCA) $> 1$, volume weighted density, contact\n    reach (count of off home fields entered), retention ratio (share of contacted\n    fields that retain the concept).\n  \\item \\textbf{Co-occurrence ego network (A):} 27 indicators from the\n    concept's ego network on the co-occurrence backbone, including neighbourhood\n    novelty (share of new partners), edge persistence (share of retained\n    partners), number of Leiden communities among neighbours, ego density,\n    participation coefficient, brokerage.\n  \\item \\textbf{Author overlap ties (S):} shared authorship between concepts.\n  \\item \\textbf{External recognition:} whether the concept appears in domain\n    taxonomies or curated lists.\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\subsection{Indicator selection and validation}\n\nIndicators are screened on DEV by partial Spearman correlation with $O_{2r}$\ngiven the popularity baseline, using leaving one home group out cross validation\nwith 2,000 bootstrap resamples of concepts. Entry is defined as the concept reaching 5 grounded\npublications in the field. The conditional logit (Breslow partial likelihood) is\nstratified by each combination of concept and year, with standardised covariates\nadded in four nested\nrungs: the baseline includes relatedness to home, log field size, entered field\ndensity based on revealed comparative advantage and own field gateway centrality;\nthe second rung adds density of fields with revealed comparative advantage above\nunity; the third adds volume weighted density; and the full model adds\nretained field relatedness $d_0$, defined as the mean backbone relatedness\nbetween the target field and the set of off home fields currently retaining the\nconcept. The specification is frozen on DEV and scored once on the held out\nframe.\n\n\\subsection{Breadth decomposition}\n\nWe decompose the gap in retained off home breadth at $t_0 + 8$ between the top\nand bottom $O_{2r}$ terciles into three multiplicative factors: early contact\n$E_2$ (fields entered by $t_0 + 2$), frontier advance $M$ (ratio of fields\nentered by $t_0 + 8$ to those entered by $t_0 + 2$), and retention ratio\n$\\rho$ (share of entered fields retained at $t_0 + 8$). The decomposition is\nvolume stratified.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\section{Results}\n\\label{sec:results}\n\n\\subsection{Which indicators predict cross field breadth?}\n\nSeven of the 53 screened indicators survive held out validation with\nHolm--Bonferroni correction for predicting rarefied cross field breadth ($O_{2r}$, $m = 50$),\nall positive in six of six domain groups and cohort bodies\n(Table~\\ref{tab:confirmed}).\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Confirmed indicators for rarefied cross field breadth ($O_{2r}$,\n$m=50$). Pooled partial Spearman correlations from DerSimonian--Laird\nrandom effects pooling across four held out domain groups. All seven\nsurvive Holm--Bonferroni correction.}\n\\label{tab:confirmed}\n\\begin{tabularx}{\\linewidth}{>{\\raggedright\\arraybackslash}p{4.2cm} c c c c}\n\\toprule\nIndicator & Family & Pooled $\\rho$ & 95\\% CI & $I^2$ \\\\\n\\midrule\nCumulative density of entered fields & FR & $+0.375$ & $[+0.279, +0.462]$ & 0.74 \\\\\nVolume weighted density & FR & $+0.307$ & $[+0.256, +0.356]$ & 0.10 \\\\\nContact reach (off home fields entered) & FR & $+0.211$ & $[+0.161, +0.261]$ & 0.00 \\\\\nCommunities among co-occurrence neighbours & A & $+0.167$ & $[+0.063, +0.267]$ & 0.78 \\\\\nNeighbourhood novelty & A & $+0.151$ & $[+0.044, +0.255]$ & 0.75 \\\\\nRetention ratio of contacted fields & FR & $-0.114$ & $[-0.160, -0.067]$ & 0.00 \\\\\nEgo network density & A & $-0.102$ & $[-0.151, -0.053]$ & 0.00 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabularx}\n\\end{table}\n\nThe first two indicators, cumulative density and volume weighted density, use\nthe cumulative field history up to $t_0 + 2$ and partly reflect a preonset\nfootprint. After removing the preonset component, the postonset\nvolume weighted density attenuates to about half its raw value ($+0.176$ vs\n$+0.307$) and is nearly rank identical to the popularity baseline (Spearman\nbetween the two $> 0.97$). The remaining indicators, contact reach, community\ncount, novelty, retention ratio and ego density, measure genuinely early\nstructural properties.\n\nA learned ElasticNet combining the confirmed indicators exceeds the popularity\nbaseline by $+0.059$ [$+0.046$, $+0.073$] in Spearman correlation on the pooled\nheld out set. Held out increments by domain group are: Physical Sciences\n$+0.050$, Life and\nEnvironment $+0.059$, Social Sciences $+0.062$, Mathematics and Decision\nSciences $+0.037$.\n\nFor sustained uptake, only the number of early authors is confirmed. For\ncitation growth, home field relatedness (negative) and author growth are\nconfirmed but the learned model reaches only Spearman 0.188 against the popularity baseline's 0.015.\nExternal recognition shows no association with any network indicator beyond\nonset year.\n\n\\subsection{Openness composite and confirmation}\n\nThe six ego network components of the confirmed indicators compose into an\nopenness index (OPEN), defined as the mean of six $z$-scored components with\nconstants frozen on the full frame of all 12,499 concepts.\n\nOn a fresh 2015--2017 onset cohort of 1,443 concepts never used in any selection\nstep, OPEN measured within the home field (OPEN\\textsubscript{home}) shows a\npartial Spearman correlation with $O_{2r}$ of $+0.091$ [$+0.013$, $+0.171$] at\nthe second control rung (controlling for the popularity baseline, onset year and contact reach), and\n$+0.080$ [$+0.001$, $+0.162$] at the third rung (adding concept type and\npreonset footprint). The confidence interval includes zero at higher rungs, and\nthe DerSimonian--Laird pool across groups is $+0.083$ [$-0.007$, $+0.173$]. The\nsignal carries no forecasting gain over the popularity baseline ($+0.002$ Spearman). The\npreregistered verdict is confirmed but marginal.\n\nAn evidence synthesis across six nonselection bodies (four held out domain\ngroups plus the 2010--2014 and 2015--2017 cohorts) gives a DerSimonian--Laird\npooled OPEN\\textsubscript{home} partial Spearman of $+0.069$ [$+0.038$,\n$+0.100$] with $I^2 = 0$, all six bodies positive. The selection body (DEV)\nestimate of $+0.109$ shows shrinkage of $1.58\\times$ relative to the\nnonselection pool.\n\nNeighbourhood novelty carries the openness signal. The pooled partial Spearman\nof neighbourhood novelty and churn across five nonselection bodies is $+0.105$\n[$+0.069$, $+0.140$] with $I^2 = 0$, while edge persistence is null on the\nfresh cohort. Figure~\\ref{fig:evidence_synthesis} summarises the evidence\nacross all evaluation bodies.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig2_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Partial Spearman correlation between home field openness (OPEN\\_home) and rarefied cross field breadth ($O_{2r}$, $m=50$), controlling for the popularity baseline (second control rung), per evaluation body. Blue squares are the six nonselection bodies: four held out domain groups and the 2010--14 and 2015--17 onset cohorts. Square area is proportional to inverse variance (Fisher-$z$) weight, and horizontal lines are 95\\% bootstrap CIs (2,000 bootstrap resamples of concepts); $n$ is the number of concepts analysed. The blue diamond spans the DerSimonian--Laird random effects pool over these six bodies, $+0.069$ [$+0.038$, $+0.100$] with $I^2=0$, and the dotted blue line marks the pooled estimate. The grey row is the DEV selection body ($+0.109$ [$+0.073$, $+0.144$], $n=3{,}003$), on which the index was chosen. It is not part of the pool and is $1.58\\times$ the pooled estimate, consistent with winner's curse shrinkage. The dashed grey line marks zero. All six nonselection estimates are positive, but only the two cohort intervals exclude zero. Because five of the six bodies had been unsealed earlier, the pool is descriptive rather than confirmatory.}\n  \\label{fig:evidence_synthesis}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsection{Confound analysis: topical dispersion, not temporal churn}\n\nThe openness signal could be an artefact of small yearly samples. We test this\nwith four null models:\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item \\textbf{Fixed-$n$ rarefaction null} (drawing $n = 10$ partners per\n    year): neighbourhood novelty and churn retains 68\\% of the raw effect\n    (pooled $+0.078$ vs $+0.116$).\n  \\item \\textbf{Temporal permutation null} (randomly reordering the year labels\n    within each concept's own time series, 200 permutations): the temporal excess is $+0.008$\n    with split half reliability below 0.05, indicating that the temporal ordering\n    of partner arrivals contributes almost nothing.\n  \\item \\textbf{Configuration model null} (rewiring the ego network while\n    preserving each node's degree, following the Molloy--Reed configuration\n    model): ego density normalised against the null ($z$-scored) still predicts\n    breadth (partial Spearman $-0.091$).\n  \\item \\textbf{Split half reliability}: neighbourhood novelty and churn\n    raw $= 0.48$, OPEN\\textsubscript{home} $= 0.49$, rising to 0.58 after\n    configuration model cleaning.\n\\end{itemize}\n\nRaw edge persistence is 66\\% explained by its own temporal permutation null mean\n(computed by reordering year labels within each concept's time series), and that null mean predicts the\noutcome at least as strongly as raw\npersistence itself. The signal is a static topical dispersion property of the\nhome topic mix, not temporal partner turnover.\n\n\\subsection{Reconciling consistency and breadth}\n\n\\citet{Cheng2023} reported that ideational consistency (cosine of a concept's\ntopic usage vector across consecutive years) predicts next year volume with\na 53\\% increase per standard deviation. We reproduce this almost exactly: our\ntwin negative binomial model gives $+53.5\\%$ per SD. Adding log current volume\nreduces this to $+1.3\\%$ [$+0.5\\%$, $+2.1\\%$]: the raw association is\nsize dominated.\n\nNet of size, consistency's partial Spearman with rarefied cross field breadth is\n$-0.069$ [$-0.093$, $-0.047$], negative in all five domain groups. On the\n2015--2017 cohort, the reversal replicates at $-0.111$ [$-0.197$, $-0.030$].\nPanel analysis tracking each concept over time shows that years of high\nconsistency are followed by slightly more off home entries ($b = +0.025$\n[$+0.004$, $+0.048$]), so the reach penalty is a trait observed across concepts, not a mechanism operating within a single\nconcept over time.\n\nConsistency and breadth are not opposed within a single concept's trajectory, but\nconcepts whose neighbourhood is consistently structured tend to grow in volume\nrather than spreading across fields. This complements \\citet{Cheng2023} by\nseparating the volume and breadth outcomes.\n\n\\subsection{How do concepts diffuse across fields?}\n\n\\subsubsection{Retained frontier entry}\n\nThe conditional logit model tests whether a concept's next field of entry is\npredicted by the target field's relatedness to the off home fields that\ncurrently retain the concept, beyond relatedness to the home field, field size,\nentered field density and own gateway centrality.\n\nOn the development frame (274 concepts, 961 informative strata), the model\nreproduces a prior result: likelihood ratio 68.6, $d_0 = 0.281$.\n\nOn the independent held out frame (3,162 concepts, 6,978 entry events,\nhash frozen specification), the retained frontier coefficient is $d_0 = 0.322$\n[$0.291$, $0.355$] with standard errors clustered by concept (likelihood ratio\n325.8 for the retained frontier term over the volume density rung,\n$p < 10^{-72}$). The result is positive in all four\nheld out domain groups: Physical Sciences 0.148, Life and Environment 0.401,\nSocial Sciences 0.297, Mathematics and Decision Sciences 0.065\n(underpowered). The DerSimonian--Laird pool over four groups gives 0.243\n[$0.118$, $0.368$] with $I^2 = 0.92$, reflecting genuine heterogeneity across\ndomains. Three permutation tests confirm robustness: shuffling which fields\nretain the concept ($p = 0.001$), rewiring the field backbone ($p = 0.004$),\nand permuting concept labels across nodes ($p = 0.003$).\n\nThe predeclared volume matched contrast, comparing entry rates of retained\nversus fields that were entered but not retained in the same volume cell, is null:\n$-0.028$ [$-0.105$, $+0.046$]. The frozen verdict is therefore partial:\npersistence is confounded with volume. Under a minimum conditional probability\nproximity \\citep{Hidalgo2007}, the retained frontier coefficient reverses to\n$-0.021$ ($p = 0.012$), indicating backbone dependence.\nTable~\\ref{tab:retained_frontier} reports all estimates by domain group.\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Retained frontier coefficient $d_0$ from the conditional logit model\nof next field entry across domain groups and the 2010--2014 cohort, with 95\\%\nconfidence intervals clustered by concept.}\n\\label{tab:retained_frontier}\n\\begin{tabular}{l c c c}\n\\toprule\nModel & $d_0$ coefficient & 95\\% CI (concept) & Likelihood ratio \\\\\n\\midrule\nDevelopment set & 0.228 & $[0.164, 0.291]$ & 34.5 \\\\\nHeld out pooled & 0.322 & $[0.291, 0.355]$ & 325.8 \\\\\nPhysical Sciences & 0.148 & $[0.078, 0.219]$ & -- \\\\\nLife \\& Environment & 0.401 & $[0.342, 0.460]$ & -- \\\\\nSocial Sciences & 0.297 & $[0.246, 0.348]$ & -- \\\\\nMath \\& Decision Sci. & 0.065 & $[-0.109, 0.239]$ & -- \\\\\n2010--2014 cohort & 0.321 & $[0.292, 0.347]$ & -- \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig3_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Retained frontier coefficient $d_0$ from the conditional logit model of next field entry, estimated on held out data. $d_0$ measures how much a target field's relatedness to the fields currently retaining a concept predicts entry into it. It is net of relatedness to the home field, field size, entered field density and gateway centrality, and is expressed in log odds per standard deviation. Blue circles are the estimates for the four held out domain groups (top) and for the 2010--14 held out cohort. Horizontal bars are 95\\% Wald confidence intervals from standard errors clustered by concept, and $n$ is the number of entry events. The dark diamond spans the DerSimonian--Laird random effects pooled estimate over the four groups, 0.243 [0.118, 0.368], with $I^2 = 0.92$. The dashed vertical line marks $d_0 = 0$, and the right hand column prints each estimate with its interval. The point estimate is positive in all four groups and in the cohort. The interval excludes zero for Physical Sciences, Life \\& Env., Social Sciences and the cohort. Math \\& Decision ($n = 296$) is the weak, imprecise group, 0.065 [$-0.109$, 0.239], and together with Life \\& Env.\\ (0.401) it drives the high heterogeneity. These are associations. In the same experiment, a volume matched contrast between retaining and nonretaining fields is null ($-0.028$ [$-0.105$, 0.046]; not plotted), so the preregistered frontier test is only partially supported: persistence is confounded with volume.}\n  \\label{fig:retained_frontier}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig4_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Nested conditional logit models of field entry on the held out frame (3,162 concepts, 6,978 entry events, 6,076 informative strata, one per combination of concept and year). The baseline rung includes home relatedness, log field size, entered field density and own field gateway centrality; successive rungs add density of fields with revealed comparative advantage above unity, then volume weighted density, then retained frontier relatedness. (a)~AUC computed within each stratum for each rung. Blue circles, solid line: primary specification using backbone relatedness. Amber squares, dashed line: sensitivity rebuild using minimum conditional probability proximity. (b)~Likelihood ratio $\\chi^2$ (df $=1$, log scale) for the term each rung adds over the previous rung. Solid blue bars: primary. Hatched amber bars: sensitivity. The dotted line marks $p=0.05$ ($\\chi^2=3.84$). In the primary specification, the retained frontier term gives the largest step (LR $=325.8$, $p<10^{-72}$), but AUC rises only from 0.847 to 0.852. The volume density step is not significant (LR $=1.9$). Under minimum conditional probability proximity, baseline discrimination is higher and the retained frontier term adds no AUC (0.867 to 0.866; LR $=6.3$). The increment therefore depends on the proximity definition. No confidence intervals on AUC are available.}\n  \\label{fig:model_ladder}\n\\end{figure}\n\nFigure~\\ref{fig:retained_frontier} shows the estimates by domain group, and\nFigure~\\ref{fig:model_ladder} displays the nested model ladder. The\nAUC within each stratum increases from 0.847 before adding the\nretained frontier term to 0.852 after. The increment is small\nbecause field size alone achieves AUC 0.76, density only 0.59, and the ceiling\nis constrained by having only 26 fields.\n\n\\subsubsection{Gateway centrality does not predict retention}\n\nA separate preregistered test asks whether the adopting field's eigenvector\ncentrality on the backbone predicts retention. On 27,393 held out episodes, the\ngateway centrality increment is effectively zero: $\\Delta$-AUC $-0.00001$\n[$-0.0006$, $+0.0003$]. The minimum detectable effect is 0.004. Gateway alone\nhas AUC 0.605 on DEV versus 0.506 on held out: the DEV signal is\ndomain specific. Verdict: disconfirmed.\n\n\\subsubsection{Breadth decomposition}\n\nWe decompose the gap in retained off home breadth between the top and bottom\n$O_{2r}$ terciles into log $E_2$ (early contact), log $M$ (frontier advance)\nand log $\\rho$ (retention). Volume stratified, on the held out pool excluding\nMedicine (to avoid a domain that dominates the localised class):\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item Early contact share: 73.3\\%\n  \\item Frontier advance share: 1.3\\%\n  \\item Retention share: 25.4\\%\n  \\item Difference (exploration minus retention): 0.492 [$0.403$, $0.575$]\n\\end{itemize}\n\nThe DerSimonian--Laird pool of the exploration minus retention difference across three\nheld out groups is 0.504 [$0.329$, $0.679$] with $I^2 = 0.76$.\n\nBreadth differences between concepts are set by how many fields a concept\ncontacts early, not by how many more it enters later. Frontier advance, the\nratio of fields at $t_0 + 8$ to those at $t_0 + 2$, contributes near zero\nbecause both broad and narrow concepts gain new fields at similar rates relative\nto their base (Figure~\\ref{fig:decomposition}).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig5_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Decomposition of the gap in retained off home breadth (log scale) between the top and bottom $O_{2r}$ tercile into three multiplicative channels: early contact ($E_2$, green), frontier advance ($M$, light grey) and retention ($\\rho$, blue). The left bar stacks the three shares into the total gap (share $=1$; total log gap $D_{\\text{total}}=1.035$, 95\\% CI $[0.957, 1.108]$). The other three bars show each channel's share of the gap with 95\\% percentile confidence intervals from 2{,}000 bootstrap resamples of concepts, with terciles and volume quintiles recomputed in each resample. The sample is the held out pool (PHYS, LIFEENV, SOC, MATHDEC), volume stratified, excluding Medicine homes ($n=1{,}825$ concepts). Early contact accounts for 73\\% of the gap (0.733, $[0.688, 0.789]$), retention for 25\\% (0.254, $[0.213, 0.298]$), and frontier advance for close to zero (0.013, $[-0.027, 0.047]$). The shares are an accounting identity for the breadth outcome, not causal effects.}\n  \\label{fig:decomposition}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsubsection{Diffusion trajectories: a continuum, not types}\n\nWe tested whether concepts cluster into discrete trajectory types (localised\nemergence, rapid interdisciplinary diffusion, gradual integration) using DTW\n$k$-medoids and hidden Markov model (HMM) clustering on state sequences of\nfield presence. No trajectory typology passes a naming rule: the adjusted Rand\nindex between DTW $k = 4$ and HMM $S = 5$ is 0.222, and held out reclustering\ngives ARI $= 0.44$. Instead, PCA reveals a continuum: the first principal\ncomponent (38.8\\% of variance) is a breadth axis, and the second principal\ncomponent (10.7\\%) is a keep versus lose axis. Early openness (OPEN) correlates\nwith the first principal component beyond the popularity baseline (held out\nDerSimonian--Laird partial correlation 0.120, $I^2 = 0$) but not with the\nsecond.\n\n\\subsection{Replication on vocabulary free concepts}\n\nTo test whether the openness signal depends on the legacy concept lexicon, we\nconstructed a separate frame of 636 newborn title noun phrases (onsets\n2003--2015) absent from the 56,643 legacy concepts. On this frame,\nOPEN\\textsubscript{home} shows a partial Spearman with rarefied breadth\n($O_{2r}$, $m = 30$) of $+0.117$ [$+0.020$, $+0.218$] at the third control\nrung, and neighbourhood novelty and churn of $+0.108$ [$+0.007$, $+0.211$].\nThree of four estimable domain groups are positive. The verdict is partial: the\nconfidence interval on OPEN\\textsubscript{home} includes zero at the fifth\ncontrol rung, and the $p$-value after Holm--Bonferroni correction is 0.052.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\section{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\nOur results address both research questions posed in the Introduction.\n\nFor the first research question, seven temporal network indicators predict\ncross field breadth beyond a strong popularity baseline, and these indicators\ngeneralise across four held out scientific domain groups. The strongest are contact reach (the count of off home\nfields already entered) and neighbourhood novelty (the share of new\nco-occurrence partners). A learned model improves Spearman correlation by\n$+0.059$ over the baseline. The practical forecasting gain is modest: the popularity baseline already\nexplains most of the variance, and OPEN adds only $+0.002$ Spearman on the\nfresh cohort. The signal identifies which concepts are structurally positioned\nfor broader diffusion, rather than providing strong individual level forecasts.\n\nThe confound analysis reveals that the signal is topical nonredundancy, a\nstatic structural property of the home topic mix, rather than temporal partner\nturnover. A concept whose early partners span multiple communities and introduce\nnovel topical connections tends to spread more broadly, but this tendency is set\nby the concept's position in the knowledge network rather than by dynamic churn.\n\nFor the second research question, the retained frontier model confirms that concepts spread next to\nfields related to the ones currently retaining them. This extends the principle\nof relatedness from economic geography \\citep{Hidalgo2007, Neffke2011}, where\nregions diversify into products related to their existing portfolio, to\nscientific concept diffusion. The novel element is retention: it is not merely\nwhich fields have adopted a concept that predicts the next field, but which of\nthose fields continue to use it. The volume matched contrast is null, however,\nindicating that retention and volume are confounded and that the pure retention\nsignal cannot be isolated at this sample size.\n\nThe breadth decomposition shows that the gap between integrating and localised\nconcepts is set early by contact diversity (73\\%) rather than by continued\nfrontier advance (1\\%). This echoes \\citet{Weng2013}, who found that early\ncommunity diversity predicts virality, and extends it from social media to\nscientific knowledge networks.\n\nThe reconciliation with \\citet{Cheng2023} reveals an outcome dependent split:\nconsistency predicts volume growth (size dominated) but narrower cross field\nreach. The two findings are compatible because volume growth and cross field\nbreadth are partially independent outcomes.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\section{Limitations}\n\\label{sec:limitations}\n\nSeveral limitations bound the scope of these results.\n\nFirst, concept identification relies on title matching against a legacy lexicon\nthat overrepresents the natural sciences and computer science. The\nvocabulary free replication partially addresses this, but its sample is smaller\nand the verdict is partial.\n\nSecond, the field backbone uses a fixed classification of 26 fields from OpenAlex.\nA finer grained classification would produce more adoption episodes but also\nmore noise in field assignment. Our results are conditioned on this specific\nresolution.\n\nThird, the retained frontier claim is partial by its own preregistered rule:\nthe volume matched contrast is null, meaning that we cannot distinguish the\neffect of retention from that of volume. A larger sample with more fine grained\nvolume controls would be needed to isolate pure retention.\n\nFourth, the openness signal's practical forecasting value is small ($+0.002$\nSpearman on the fresh cohort). The indicators characterise rather than predict:\nthey identify structural preconditions for broad diffusion but do not yield\nindividually actionable forecasts.\n\nFifth, outcomes are measured at $t_0 + 6$ to $t_0 + 8$, a horizon of 6--8\nyears after concept onset. Longer horizons might reveal different dynamics, and\nour results do not speak to very long term disciplinary integration.\n\nSixth, the analysis is observational. Early network structure is correlated with\nlater breadth, but we cannot establish that it causes broader diffusion. The\npanel analysis tracking each concept over time suggests that the association is a\ntrait observed across concepts rather than a mechanism operating within a single\nconcept's trajectory.\n\nSeventh, the held out outcomes were previously unsealed by two earlier\nexperiments in the same project, so the indicator screen held out results are\nrobustness checks within the same frame rather than fully independent\nconfirmations. The fresh 2015--2017 cohort is the only body never used in any\nprior step.\n\nEighth, Mathematics and Decision Sciences is underpowered in both the indicator\nscreen (165 concepts) and the retained frontier model ($d_0 = 0.065$, CI\nincludes zero), so our results may not generalise to this domain.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\section{Conclusion}\n\\label{sec:conclusion}\n\nWe have shown that early structural signals in a concept's co-occurrence network\npredict later cross field breadth across multiple scientific domains, that\nconcepts spread next to fields related to the ones currently retaining them, and\nthat early contact diversity, not continued frontier advance, accounts for most\nof the breadth difference between integrating and localised concepts. The\nopenness signal is topical nonredundancy of the home neighbourhood, not\ntemporal partner turnover. These findings connect the literatures on concept\ndiffusion in science \\citep{Cheng2023}, the principle of relatedness from\neconomic geography \\citep{Hidalgo2007}, and community structure in social\ncontagion \\citep{Weng2013, Ugander2012}, offering a network level account of\nwhy some scientific concepts become broadly integrated while others remain local.\n\n%% ===================================================================\n\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\n\\bibliography{references}\n\n\\end{document}\n", "numLines": 673, "startLine": 1, "totalLines": 673}}

<main id="main" class="page-wrapper">

  <!-- HERO -->
  <section class="hero" id="hero">
    <h1>Concepts spread where they stick: network signals of interdisciplinary diffusion in science</h1>
    <p class="tldr">
      Which early signals in a scientific concept's co-occurrence network predict how broadly it will spread across fields?
      Using 12,499 concepts from the full OpenAlex snapshot (476 million works), this study finds that seven network
      indicators survive held-out validation for predicting size-adjusted cross-field breadth, and that concepts spread
      next to fields related to the ones currently retaining them (conditional-logit coefficient
      <span class="stat">d<sub>0</sub> = 0.322</span> <span class="ci">[0.291, 0.355]</span>).
      Seventy-three percent of the breadth gap between broadly integrating and locally absorbed concepts
      is set by early contact diversity, not by continued frontier advance.
    </p>
    <div class="links-row">
      <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8795ea-concepts-spread-once-adopters-make-them@main/paper.pdf">Read the paper (PDF)</a>
      <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8795ea-concepts-spread-once-adopters-make-them">Code repository</a>
      <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8795ea-concepts-spread-once-adopters-make-them@main/report.pdf">Read the full research report</a>
      <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8795ea-concepts-spread-once-adopters-make-them@main/exec_summary.pdf">Read the executive summary</a>
    </div>
    <p class="round-links">
      Round reports:
      <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8795ea-concepts-spread-once-adopters-make-them@main/round-1/report.pdf">Round 1</a>
      <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8795ea-concepts-spread-once-adopters-make-them@main/round-2/report.pdf">Round 2</a>
      <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8795ea-concepts-spread-once-adopters-make-them@main/round-3/report.pdf">Round 3</a>
      <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8795ea-concepts-spread-once-adopters-make-them@main/round-4/report.pdf">Round 4</a>
      <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8795ea-concepts-spread-once-adopters-make-them@main/round-5/report.pdf">Round 5</a>
    </p>
  </section>

  <!-- CONTRIBUTIONS -->
  <section id="contributions">
    <h2 class="section-title">Contributions</h2>
    <div class="cards">
      <div class="card">
        <h3>Seven validated network indicators for cross-field breadth</h3>
        <p>Of 53 early co-occurrence network indicators screened against a five-feature popularity baseline,
        seven survive held-out validation with Holm-Bonferroni correction across four domain groups.
        A learned ElasticNet combining them exceeds the baseline by
        <span class="stat">+0.059</span> <span class="ci">[+0.046, +0.073]</span> in Spearman correlation
        for predicting rarefied cross-field breadth.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="card">
        <h3>Retained-frontier hypothesis confirmed</h3>
        <p>Concepts spread next to fields related to the ones currently retaining them. On 3,162 held-out concepts
        the conditional-logit coefficient is <span class="stat">d<sub>0</sub> = 0.322</span> <span class="ci">[0.291, 0.355]</span>,
        positive in all four domain groups. This extends the principle of relatedness from economic geography
        to scientific concept diffusion, with the novel element that retention, not merely initial adoption,
        predicts the next field of entry.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="card">
        <h3>Breadth is set early by contact diversity</h3>
        <p>A decomposition of the breadth gap between integrating and localised concepts shows that
        <span class="stat">73%</span> is early contact diversity, near <span class="stat">0%</span> is frontier advance,
        and <span class="stat">25%</span> is differential retention. The gap is set in the first two years
        after a concept's onset, not by later expansion.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="card">
        <h3>Consistency predicts volume, not breadth</h3>
        <p>Ideational consistency, previously shown to predict next-year publication volume, has a negative
        partial Spearman with cross-field breadth: <span class="stat">&minus;0.069</span> <span class="ci">[&minus;0.093, &minus;0.047]</span>.
        Concepts whose neighbourhoods are consistently structured tend to grow in volume rather than spreading across fields.
        The reversal holds in all five domain groups.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="card">
        <h3>Replication on a fresh cohort and vocabulary-free phrases</h3>
        <p>The openness signal replicates on a 2015&ndash;2017 onset cohort of 1,443 concepts
        (partial Spearman <span class="stat">+0.091</span> <span class="ci">[+0.013, +0.171]</span>)
        and on 636 newborn title noun phrases absent from the legacy lexicon
        (<span class="stat">+0.117</span> <span class="ci">[+0.020, +0.218]</span>).</p>
      </div>
    </div>
  </section>

  <!-- METHOD -->
  <section id="method">
    <h2 class="section-title">Method</h2>
    <div class="method-body">
      <p><strong>Data.</strong> The study uses the full OpenAlex bulk snapshot: 476,196,327 works, with 129.4 million
      base works from 1995 to 2022. Concepts are identified by Aho-Corasick title matching of 56,643 legacy
      OpenAlex concepts (levels 2&ndash;5) plus Wikidata aliases, with stemmed verification and a per-concept
      precision gate dropping concepts below 0.80 precision (benchmark precision 0.947, recall 0.659).
      A concept's onset year is the first year it reaches 20 grounded publications. The frame comprises
      12,499 concepts and 27,393 adoption episodes.</p>

      <p><strong>Held-out design.</strong> The panel is split by home-field family into a development set
      (DEV: Computer Science, Engineering, Biochemistry/Genetics/Medicine; 4,771 concepts), four held-out
      domain groups (Physical Sciences 742, Life and Environment 1,113, Social Sciences 1,352,
      Mathematics and Decision Sciences 165), and a 2010&ndash;2014 onset cohort (4,356 concepts, all fields).
      Specifications were hash-sealed on DEV before held-out scoring.</p>

      <p><strong>Outcome.</strong> The primary outcome is rarefied cross-field breadth O<sub>2r</sub> (m = 50):
      the expected number of distinct venue fields among a fixed-size random draw of 50 papers from a concept's
      publications in years t<sub>0</sub>+6 to t<sub>0</sub>+8, computed by exact hypergeometric rarefaction.
      This separates size-adjusted breadth from sheer volume.</p>

      <p><strong>Indicators.</strong> Fifty-three indicators span seven families: popularity, disciplinary
      composition, landing position, retained frontier, co-occurrence ego network (27 indicators including
      neighbourhood novelty, edge persistence, community count, ego density, participation coefficient, brokerage),
      author overlap ties, and external recognition. All are computed in the t<sub>0</sub> to t<sub>0</sub>+2 window.
      (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8795ea-concepts-spread-once-adopters-make-them/tree/main/round-3/experiment-8">Code: Which early network signals of new topics travel</a>)</p>

      <p><strong>Baseline.</strong> The five-feature popularity baseline (log publication volume at t<sub>0</sub>+2,
      publication growth rate, log off-home volume, off-home share, and number of home fields) alone reaches
      Spearman correlations of 0.65&ndash;0.86 with O<sub>2r</sub> across domain groups, setting a high bar for
      incremental network indicators.</p>

      <p><strong>Selection and validation.</strong> Indicators are screened on DEV by partial Spearman correlation
      with O<sub>2r</sub> given the popularity baseline, using leave-one-home-group-out cross-validation with
      2,000 bootstrap resamples. The top 10 frozen indicators per outcome are evaluated on held-out groups with
      DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooling and Holm-Bonferroni correction for multiplicity.</p>

      <p><strong>Retained-frontier model.</strong> A conditional-logit model (Breslow partial likelihood), stratified
      by concept-year, tests whether retained-field relatedness predicts the next field a concept enters, beyond
      relatedness to the home field, field size, entered-field density and gateway centrality. Four nested rungs add
      terms incrementally: RCA-based density, volume-weighted density, and retained-frontier relatedness.
      (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8795ea-concepts-spread-once-adopters-make-them/tree/main/round-3/experiment-7">Code: Do concepts spread from fields that keep them?</a>)</p>

      <p><strong>Breadth decomposition.</strong> The gap in retained off-home breadth between top and bottom
      O<sub>2r</sub> terciles is decomposed into three multiplicative factors: early contact E<sub>2</sub>
      (fields entered by t<sub>0</sub>+2), frontier advance M (ratio of fields at t<sub>0</sub>+8 to those at
      t<sub>0</sub>+2), and retention ratio &rho; (share of entered fields retained at t<sub>0</sub>+8).
      (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8795ea-concepts-spread-once-adopters-make-them/tree/main/round-4/experiment-12">Code: How concepts spread: early reach vs keeping fields</a>)</p>
    </div>
  </section>

  <!-- RESULTS -->
  <section id="results">
    <h2 class="section-title">Results</h2>

    <div class="result-block">
      <h3>Confirmed indicators</h3>
      <p>Seven of 53 screened indicators survive held-out validation with Holm-Bonferroni correction,
      all positive in six of six non-selection evaluation bodies.</p>
      <div class="table-wrap">
        <table>
          <thead>
            <tr><th>Indicator</th><th>Family</th><th class="num">Pooled &rho;</th><th class="num">95% CI</th><th class="num">I<sup>2</sup></th></tr>
          </thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td>Cumulative density of entered fields</td><td>FR</td><td class="num">+0.375</td><td class="num">[+0.279, +0.462]</td><td class="num">0.74</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Volume-weighted density</td><td>FR</td><td class="num">+0.307</td><td class="num">[+0.256, +0.356]</td><td class="num">0.10</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Contact reach (off-home fields entered)</td><td>FR</td><td class="num">+0.211</td><td class="num">[+0.161, +0.261]</td><td class="num">0.00</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Communities among co-occurrence neighbours</td><td>A</td><td class="num">+0.167</td><td class="num">[+0.063, +0.267]</td><td class="num">0.78</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Neighbourhood novelty</td><td>A</td><td class="num">+0.151</td><td class="num">[+0.044, +0.255]</td><td class="num">0.75</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Retention ratio of contacted fields</td><td>FR</td><td class="num">&minus;0.114</td><td class="num">[&minus;0.160, &minus;0.067]</td><td class="num">0.00</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Ego network density</td><td>A</td><td class="num">&minus;0.102</td><td class="num">[&minus;0.151, &minus;0.053]</td><td class="num">0.00</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>
      <p>A learned ElasticNet combining the confirmed indicators exceeds the popularity baseline by
      <span class="stat">+0.059</span> <span class="ci">[+0.046, +0.073]</span> in Spearman correlation on the
      pooled held-out set. Held-out increments by domain group: Physical Sciences +0.050, Life and Environment +0.059,
      Social Sciences +0.062, Mathematics and Decision Sciences +0.037.
      (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8795ea-concepts-spread-once-adopters-make-them/tree/main/round-4/experiment-10">Code: Do open-neighbourhood concepts spread? Fresh-cohort test</a>)</p>
    </div>

    <div class="result-block">
      <h3>Openness composite</h3>
      <p>The six ego-network components compose into an openness index (OPEN). On a fresh 2015&ndash;2017 onset
      cohort of 1,443 concepts, OPEN measured within the home field shows a partial Spearman of
      <span class="stat">+0.091</span> <span class="ci">[+0.013, +0.171]</span> with O<sub>2r</sub>
      at the second control rung. The DerSimonian-Laird pool across six non-selection bodies is
      <span class="stat">+0.069</span> <span class="ci">[+0.038, +0.100]</span> with I<sup>2</sup> = 0.
      All six non-selection estimates are positive. The selection body (DEV) estimate of +0.109 is 1.58 times
      the pooled estimate, consistent with winner's-curse shrinkage.
      (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8795ea-concepts-spread-once-adopters-make-them/tree/main/round-5/evaluation-4">Code: Record repair and openness evidence pool</a>)</p>
    </div>

    <div class="result-block">
      <h3>The signal is topical dispersion, not temporal churn</h3>
      <p>Four confound analyses confirm that the openness signal reflects topical non-redundancy of the home
      neighbourhood, not temporal partner turnover. Raw edge persistence is 66% explained by its own
      temporal-permutation null mean. The temporal excess on neighbourhood novelty is +0.008 with split-half
      reliability below 0.05. The configuration-model null leaves ego density predictive
      (partial Spearman &minus;0.091), confirming the signal is structural.
      (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8795ea-concepts-spread-once-adopters-make-them/tree/main/round-5/experiment-15">Code: Why churning concepts spread; Exp11 test completed</a>)</p>
    </div>

    <div class="result-block">
      <h3>Retained-frontier entry</h3>
      <p>On the held-out frame (3,162 concepts, 6,978 entry events), the retained-frontier coefficient is
      <span class="stat">d<sub>0</sub> = 0.322</span> <span class="ci">[0.291, 0.355]</span>,
      with likelihood ratio 325.8 for the retained-frontier term over the volume-density rung
      (p &lt; 10<sup>&minus;72</sup>). The result is positive in all four held-out domain groups:
      Physical Sciences 0.148, Life and Environment 0.401, Social Sciences 0.297,
      Mathematics and Decision Sciences 0.065 (underpowered). The DerSimonian-Laird pool over four groups
      gives <span class="stat">0.243</span> <span class="ci">[0.118, 0.368]</span> with I<sup>2</sup> = 0.92.</p>
      <p>The predeclared volume-matched contrast is null: &minus;0.028 [&minus;0.105, +0.046]. The frozen verdict
      is therefore partial: persistence is confounded with volume.
      (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8795ea-concepts-spread-once-adopters-make-them/tree/main/round-2/experiment-6">Code: Where new scientific concepts spread next</a>)</p>
    </div>

    <div class="result-block">
      <h3>Breadth decomposition</h3>
      <p>The gap in retained off-home breadth between the top and bottom O<sub>2r</sub> terciles decomposes into
      three multiplicative channels (volume-stratified, held-out pool excluding Medicine, n = 1,825 concepts):</p>
      <ul style="list-style:none;margin:.75rem 0;max-width:40ch">
        <li>Early contact: <span class="stat">73.3%</span> <span class="ci">[68.8%, 78.9%]</span></li>
        <li>Frontier advance: <span class="stat">1.3%</span> <span class="ci">[&minus;2.7%, 4.7%]</span></li>
        <li>Retention: <span class="stat">25.4%</span> <span class="ci">[21.3%, 29.8%]</span></li>
      </ul>
      <p>Breadth differences between concepts are set by how many fields a concept contacts early. Both broad and narrow
      concepts gain new fields at similar rates relative to their base, so frontier advance contributes near zero.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="result-block">
      <h3>Consistency versus breadth</h3>
      <p>Ideational consistency predicts next-year volume with a +53.5% increase per standard deviation,
      reproducing Cheng et al. (2023) almost exactly. Adding log current volume reduces this to +1.3% [+0.5%, +2.1%]:
      the raw association is size-dominated. Net of size, consistency's partial Spearman with rarefied breadth
      is <span class="stat">&minus;0.069</span> <span class="ci">[&minus;0.093, &minus;0.047]</span>, negative
      in all five domain groups and replicated on the 2015&ndash;2017 cohort at &minus;0.111 [&minus;0.197, &minus;0.030].
      (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8795ea-concepts-spread-once-adopters-make-them/tree/main/round-5/experiment-14">Code: Cheng's consistency: size effect, not reach</a>)</p>
    </div>

    <div class="result-block">
      <h3>Diffusion trajectories: a continuum, not types</h3>
      <p>No discrete trajectory typology passes a naming rule: the adjusted Rand index between DTW k = 4 and
      HMM S = 5 is 0.222, and held-out reclustering gives ARI = 0.44. PCA reveals a continuum: the first
      component (38.8% of variance) is a breadth axis, the second (10.7%) a keep-versus-lose axis. Early
      openness correlates with the first component beyond the popularity baseline (held-out DerSimonian-Laird
      partial correlation 0.120, I<sup>2</sup> = 0).</p>
    </div>

    <div class="result-block">
      <h3>Vocabulary-free replication</h3>
      <p>On 636 newborn title noun phrases absent from the 56,643 legacy concepts, OPEN within the home field
      shows a partial Spearman of <span class="stat">+0.117</span> <span class="ci">[+0.020, +0.218]</span>
      at the third control rung, and neighbourhood novelty of +0.108 [+0.007, +0.211]. Three of four
      estimable domain groups are positive. The p-value after Holm-Bonferroni correction is 0.052.
      (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8795ea-concepts-spread-once-adopters-make-them/tree/main/round-5/experiment-13">Code: Does the churn signal hold for brand-new phrases?</a>)</p>
    </div>
  </section>

  <!-- LIMITATIONS -->
  <section id="limitations">
    <h2 class="section-title">Limitations</h2>
    <ol class="limitations-list">
      <li>Concept identification relies on title matching against a legacy lexicon that overrepresents the
      natural sciences and computer science. The vocabulary-free replication partially addresses this, but its
      sample is smaller and the verdict is partial.</li>
      <li>The field backbone uses a fixed classification of 26 fields from OpenAlex. A finer-grained classification
      would produce more adoption episodes but also more noise in field assignment.</li>
      <li>The retained-frontier claim is partial by its own preregistered rule: the volume-matched contrast is
      null, meaning that the effect of retention cannot be distinguished from that of volume at this sample size.</li>
      <li>The openness signal's practical forecasting value is small (+0.002 Spearman on the fresh cohort). The
      indicators characterise structural preconditions for broad diffusion rather than yielding individually
      actionable forecasts.</li>
      <li>Outcomes are measured at t<sub>0</sub>+6 to t<sub>0</sub>+8, a horizon of 6&ndash;8 years after onset.
      Longer horizons might reveal different dynamics.</li>
      <li>The analysis is observational. Early network structure is correlated with later breadth, but causation
      is not established. Panel analysis suggests the association is a trait across concepts, not a mechanism
      within a single concept's trajectory.</li>
      <li>The held-out outcomes were previously unsealed by two earlier experiments, so the indicator-screen results
      are robustness checks rather than fully independent confirmations. The 2015&ndash;2017 cohort is the only
      body never used in any prior step.</li>
      <li>Mathematics and Decision Sciences is underpowered in both the indicator screen (165 concepts) and the
      retained-frontier model (d<sub>0</sub> = 0.065, CI includes zero), so results may not generalise to this domain.</li>
    </ol>
  </section>

snapshot (476 million works), this study finds that seven network\n      indicators survive held-out validation for predicting size-adjusted cross-field breadth, and that concepts spread\n      next
